title: Sharing economy

definition.text: An economic system in which people share in making, distributing, trading and using goods and services, often through online platforms.

facts.text: It puts the spare capacity of goods and services to use; the classic example is that the average car sits unused 95% of the time.
It can be run by non-profits, like a lending library, or by companies for profit, such as Uber and Airbnb.
It can reduce environmental harm by cutting the number of goods that must be produced.
There is no consensus on its definition.
Critics say platforms avoid taxes, regulation and insurance costs and can cause a 'race to the bottom' in wages.
Whether its workers should be treated as independent contractors or employees is debated.

contested_note: Its labour effects and whether its gains come from real efficiency or from avoiding regulation are disputed.

definition.text: A systemic approach to using and reusing materials more productively across their whole life cycle.

facts.text: Global raw material use rose during the 20th century at about twice the rate of population growth.
Each 1 percent rise in GDP has raised raw material use by 0.4 percent.
Unlike waste management, which deals only with end-of-life waste, it covers the whole life cycle and holds every industry and consumer in it responsible.
The OECD and the US EPA have adopted it; the OECD issued a policy brief on it in 2012.

definition.text: The conventional 'take-make-waste' economy in which resources are extracted, made into products, used and thrown away.

facts.text: Its processes use up finite reserves to make short-lived products that end in landfills or incinerators.
It puts great pressure on the environment through extraction, energy-intensive production and large amounts of waste.
The circular economy and circular fashion are defined in contrast to it.
